en: In the Sanskrit language: *Cintāmaṇḍala-sādhana-nāma*. In the Tibetan language: *Dbu bcad ma'i sgrub thabs zhes bya ba* (The Sadhana of the Severed-Headed One). Homage to the glorious Vajraḍākinī! To the Blessed Lady Phag mo, the Bestower of Bliss, who stands firmly with her right leg extended, having abandoned the three realms, the three natures, and the three [poisons]—to her I perpetually prostrate. Just as according to the oral instructions of the Guru, for the one belonging to the three realms...

Because it is his very nature, he radiates the light of the youthful sun; I shall now describe his sādhana. Whether at a place marked by a single sign, in a charnel ground, or in an empty house, the yogin should always practice the accomplishment of that Vidyā who brings the three worlds to an end. Seated upon a soft bolster or on any other soft seat, and remaining properly supported therein, one should accomplish the supreme siddhi.

Next, with the three-syllable mantra, one should perform the purification (*saṃskāra*) of the offering substances with consecrated samaya-water. Having performed the ritual bathing (*snāna*) with that very same mantra, one should subsequently don the armor (*kavaca*). Grasping all the limbs and joints with the left hand, one should [visualize] the syllables of the mantra: *Oṃ Bāṃ Hāṃ Yāṃ Hrīṃ Māṃ Hreṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ Phaṭ*.

With the tip of the left hand, first pressing firmly from the navel upward, recite these three [mantras]: Oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho ’ham. Oṃ vajraśuddhāḥ sarvadharmā vajraśuddho ’ham. Oṃ yogaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmā yogaśuddho ’ham.
Following that, the wise one should generate pride for the sake of purifying the three realms, while remaining poised equally in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
In that same manner, within those eight charnel grounds, one should meditate upon the three places while remaining in equipoise through the yoga of swift forms;
having visualized that, one should then radiate rays of light.
Having illuminated the beings wandering through the three realms of existence, he shall lead them back once more.
From the Radiance of the Light Rays,
having clearly illuminated the sentient beings dwelling in the three realms, one should then again withdraw [them] and dissolve the entire universe into emptiness on all sides.
Resembling pure crystal, he is the embodiment of non-dual knowledge.
From the Meditation on the Initial Condensation: "One should make all variety empty;

through purity, it is the nature of non-dual gnosis, like a crystal. One should recite the mantra of the Victorious One, whose intrinsic nature is emptiness and so forth. *tattvaṃ paṭhej jinamantraṃ śūnyatādisvabhāvakam*.
Then, one should meditate upon a red lotus arising from the syllable Hrīḥ in the intermediate space.
Furthermore, through the emptiness that follows [the previous stage] and so forth, by the natural power of the blessings of the Conqueror’s mantras,
one should then meditate upon space arising from a red syllable *hrīḥ*.
Above that, one should meditate on the mandalas of the moon, sun, and fire.
In the center of that, one should again meditate upon her who resembles the syllable Vaṃ and the universe.
Furthermore, one should meditate upon what is to be visualized above that: look at the moon, the sun, and fire;
there, one should also meditate upon a maṇḍala, like the syllable Bāṃ of various colors. Then, one should see a curved knife born from the syllable Vaṃ, adorned with the seed-syllable.
One should meditate upon oneself as Vajrayoginī, transformed into the form of Karttikā.

Then, one should visualize the one born from the syllable *Bām*, adorned with curved knives. One should meditate on the complete transformation of those curved knives; through this emanation, the yogin himself [becomes] the threefold form possessing three colors. *sphaṇarayed ātmanā yogī trayarūpāṃ trivarṇiṇīm* | 13ab |*
[She is] green, yellowish-red, and red, holding a curved knife and a skull-cup.

The Vajrayoginī has three forms and possesses three colors: green, red, and yellow; she holds a curved knife and a skull-cup, with her hair loose and flowing, naked, three-eyed, and with circular red [eyes].
Endowed with fresh youth and adorned with the five mudrās.
With his tongue protruding and his voice like that of a camel, possessing three eyes that are red and round, endowed with the youthfulness of a young man, and adorned with the five mudrās;
two-armed and one-faced, divine, and radiant with a terrible, loud laugh.
She is terrible, with her feet playfully extended, and adorned with a long garland of severed heads.
Beautiful with one face and two arms, laughing fiercely and wrathfully, her right leg extended in a terrifying posture of bliss, and her garland of heads beautifully arranged;
she holds a vajra-knife as a weapon, cutting and hanging over the shoulders.
In the right [hand] is a vajra-knife, and in the left is a moistened severed head.
Having severed my head with a vajra-kartṛka, he holds it above his body;
with his right hand he holds a vajra-kartṛka, and with his left he covers half of his hair.
*Muṇḍopari karoṭaṃ ca adhomukhaṃ mukhāvṛtam*.
She holds a khaṭvāṅga staff, is yellow in color, and resembles saffron-red;
with a skull-cup upon her head and half of her hair held down, her face is turned downward; she is yellow and possesses a khaṭvāṅga equal in hue to saffron-red.
The knower of yoga should always meditate upon her as being overtaken by the Night of Time (Kālarātri).
Carrying three streams of blood resembling the hollows of the moon and sun,
the yogi should always meditate upon them as being evenly balanced. Blood flows from the three channels like the moon, the sun, and the sky.
The triple channel issuing forth from the left, right, and middle [channels].
One should constantly meditate upon the upward-moving Avadhūtī as she drinks.
One should meditate on [the wind] constantly emerging from the three channels— the left, the right, and likewise the middle; the *ābaddhūtī* moves upward.
The three channels are formed by means of the forms of body, speech, and mind.
The two channels of the left and right should likewise be meditated upon quickly;
by way of being the nature of Body, Speech, and Mind, they abide as the essence of the three channels.
*Lalanā* abides as the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), and *rasanā* as the means (*upāya*).
The Avadhūtī, however, is in the middle region, having the form of the nature of great bliss.
Wisdom (prajñā) abides as the essence, while means (upāya) abides as the flavor;
the central abode, the *ābaddhūtī*, is the nature of the various forms of great bliss.
Having meditated upon this triple-junction (*trisandhi*) with the *tāyā*, one is like a jewel of manifold forms. o ||
Meditate on this during the three junctions of the day; various forms are like precious jewels.
Now I shall explain the extraction of the mantra exactly and in proper sequence:
the practitioner, staying in a pure place, should then recite the mantra.
Just as in the sequence of before and after, one should then explain the mantra. Having resided in a pure location and recited the mantra,
first [one should recite] three times the number of the Vedas (thirty-six), and then the thirty-two [syllables] considered [as the core].
The twenty-third [digit] and the twenty-seventh are above the head.

One should first establish the direct perception of the ritual; take the thirty-first of the desires, and likewise the twenty-third and the twenty-seventh above the head. Trayoviṃśati-praṇaḥ grāhyaḥ, pañcamaṃ cāpy adho-yutam.
Having extracted the syllable *tha* from the back of *da*, it is also joined below by the back of *da*.
Furthermore, the twenty-third [letter] is to be taken; the five vowel-syllables are to be joined below it.
The letter following *tha* is also to be correctly taken and joined below the letter following *da*. Then the thirteenth [letter] is to be given, adorned with the second vowel.
Having extracted the first letter, it is joined with the third vowel.

After that, one should give the thirteenth [consonant] as the object of offering; it should be correctly combined with the second vowel. Having taken the first letter, it should be joined with the third vowel. Then one should provide the twentieth [consonant], adorned with the fourth vowel.
Then, twenty-six [units] should be taken, together with eleven.
Give the twentieth [letter] and adorn it with the fourth vowel;
then take the twenty-sixth and join it with the eleventh.
Furthermore, the twenty-third should be given, and the eighth is extracted.
Having given twenty-three and taken eight, one should take the twenty-seventh joined with the twenty-ninth;
the peak is considered to be fifteen, and the head is twenty-seven.

The twenty-seventh should be joined at the end; it is incomplete by one of the thirty-one. The fifteenth should be placed as an insertion. The twenty-seventh is to be set at the head. Furthermore, the back [of the seal] should be provided, adorned even with the fourth.
Ten thousand of the class of vowels (the *ravarga*) should be taken and divided by eleven.
Alternatively, one should provide a support for the back and adorn it with the fourth [vowel];
holding the lower letter *ra*, one should adorn it with the eleventh [vowel].
Furthermore, one should give the twenty-third [consonant], which is the third of the *ca*-group.
Having extracted the back of the letter Pha, which is joined with the twenty-seventh [consonant] below and situated within the twelve vowels.

Alternatively, one should take the twenty-third letter from *tza*, and to that third [letter] counted from *tza*, one should join the twenty-seventh [letter] from below; having taken the letter from behind the father (*pha*), it should be adorned with the twelfth vowel.
*pakārasya saptamaṃ grāhyaṃ trayodaśavibheditam* |
The sixth, second, and tenth [syllables] should be given, adorned with the seed-syllable of Māyā.
On the seventh counted from *pa*, one should adorn it with the thirteenth;
one should provide the sixth of the second decade and adorn it with the seed-syllable of illusion (*māyā*).
Then one should give the seed-syllable of wind (*vāyu*) endowed with the eleventh.
The thirty-three [syllables] multiplied by three, joined with the sixth vowel.
Following that, provide the seed-syllable of wind; it should be endowed with the eleventh vowel.
As for the thirtieth, it should be counted three times. The sixth vowel should be joined [with it]. [The mantra is: *nā* together with the *bindu*, joined with three *phaṭ*s.
One should then know the utterance of "svāhā" as the mantra that brings complete accomplishment.

In the *nāḍī* [channel] which is perfectly pure, one should join the syllable *phaṭ* three times; thereafter, one should bestow *svāhā*. Having meditated on the garland of rays devoid of parts at the secret place, the wise one [should recite] the mantra of the perfectly complete siddhi.
One should recite the supreme mantra by means of the yoga of emanation and reabsorption.
In the secret place of the wise, one should meditate on the three-fold garland of *ni* syllables;
through the yoga of emanation and reabsorption, the supreme mantra should be correctly recited.
The yogin should employ the illuminator of mantras according to the specific rite.
It must be guarded with great effort and not given to just anyone.

The yoga that clarifies the mantras should be applied according to the ritual procedures; it must be kept secret with great effort, like a pregnant woman concealing her condition from anyone other than her husband. *Sujaptaṃ caiva kartavyaṃ jananījāragarbhavat* (And it should be well-recited, like the child of a woman’s paramour).
A gift should be given only after thorough examination; it should not be given to one who has not been examined.
To whomever and for whatever purpose it is not to be given, one should give it only after careful examination,
keeping it strictly secret. One must not give it to those who are disrespectful,
deceitful, fierce, or who disparage other masters and gurus.
[It should not be given] to one devoid of devotion, to the deceitful, to the cruel, or to one who reviles the teacher and the guru;
rather, it should always be given to those devoted to the guru, free from doubt, and ever delighted in dharma.
One who lacks generosity and has great conceptualization should not give after having analyzed [the recipient].
One who lacks devotion to the guru and is devoid of discernment, though always delighting in the Dharma and pure, [is unsuitable].
One who possesses the complete oral instructions, is patient, and is highly intelligent;
The extracted mantra, born from the union with the Siddhi-yoginīs, should be bestowed. || 1 ||
To those who have purified their minds, who possess patience and intelligence, and for whom the yoga of practice has been taught, I shall bestow this collection of mantras.
Now, I shall explain the procedure for worship according to the essence of the practitioners of yoga.
The navel-maṇḍala is the syllable E, adorned with the three qualities (guṇas) as its mark.
Following the Yogācāra tradition, the ritual of worship is now explained:
it is encircled by three garlands and marked by a triple revolution.
The mantra, complete with its accomplishments (*siddhi*), is entwined by the three channels (*nāḍī*).
The yogi should contemplate this a hundred times, especially at the time of worship: "In the mandala of the well-perfected and accomplished [deity], the mantra is recited;
the yogi constantly contemplates it, particularly at the time of offering."
On the tenth and eighth lunar days of both the bright and dark fortnights, as well as on the fourteenth,
one should perform worship with the five offerings using the *avasavya* (anti-clockwise) method.
On the tenth day of the bright or dark fortnight, or on the eighth or the fourteenth, one should perform worship with the five offerings, using the left hand for the offering:
namely, solid food, soft food, and likewise drinks, as well as the outer and secret worship.
In a vessel made of gold or other materials, properly smeared with red sandalwood paste.
Likewise, offer food, feasts, and drinks; similarly, with outer, inner, and secret offerings,
and well-anointed with red sandalwood, saffron, agarwood, and camphor— perfumed with saffron, agarwood, and camphor— with the water of commitment (samayodaka).
The finest powder of vermilion becomes greyish when rubbed with a cloth.
The master, having purified the pledge-water, should place fine *sindūra* powder inside a cloth and, with a golden stylus, draw the *dharmodayā* there in a vessel made of gold or other materials.
In the center, however, the king of mantras should be well-inscribed in three garlands.
With a probe made of gold, the wise one should properly draw three garlands of the King of Mantras in the center of the source of phenomena (dharmodaya).
Outside, there wanders a terrible [serpent] of universal color and great luster.
And at the three junctions of the day, he should remain well-concealed with his hair unbound.
Externally, the world is wretched with cyclic existence; internally, various [fires] blaze intensely.
With great secrecy, at all three times, having shorn one's hair and gone naked, the mantra practitioner, always composed in meditative absorption, should contemplate while facing westward.
It should be worshipped with diligence for the sake of attaining accomplishment and liberation.
The mantrin, facing west, relying with effort upon meditative concentration,
should worship with diligence for the sake of liberation and accomplishment,
using flowers, incense, fragrant scents, and so forth... [lost]

Incense and fragrant substances, and likewise well-prepared divine food offerings; *āli-phalgu* and *phag-dra-ne*, *kha-che* sandalwood and red sandalwood, as well as fragrant sandalwood; likewise *aśoka* flowers, *kumuda*, *nāgakeśara*, and various other flowers—beautiful in color and sweet in scent; *daru* flowers and fruits, with threads and fully blossomed flowers, [I] offer as worship.

The places for the activities should be honored in their proper order with fragrant incense and flowers; having bowed and offered praise, one should request forbearance. Then, the yogin likewise gratifies the Youthful One (Kumāra). For the sake of accomplishing the purpose of yoga, the mantra of the *bali* offering should be recited: Oṃ Ārāli Hoḥ, Jaḥ Hūṃ Baṃ Hoḥ.

Recite three times: *vajradākini samayas tvāṃ dṛśya ho*. One should recite it four or five times. In successive and non-successive order, one should offer [the skull-cup]. Opening the vajra-palms upward, one should recite this mantra: *oṃ khakhāhi khāhi sarvayakṣarākṣasabhūtapretapiśāca audumbara āpasmāra*.

*Dākinīyadaya ai māṃ bālīṃ gṛhṇa mama samayarakṣāṃ duryathai yāṃ ṣṭāṃ bhūnyatha pi tha dzi ghra tha mātikratha mama sarvakartaya satsu khāṃ bi phri ddha ye sa hayika bhandu hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.* On the eighth and the fourteenth [days], offer this three times during the intervals [of the day]. Even for those of inferior intellect, this is the method of accomplishment.

Having extracted [the essence] from the *Sdom brgya mtsos*, this method for accomplishing the goal (*don sgrub thabs*) was composed by Bari. Although the words and letters are not perfectly complete, it is fitting that the ḍākinīs grant their forbearance. This must be kept as a most secret and strictly concealed instruction, far more secret than the secret instructions of the yoginīs. The *Sādhana of Severed-Headed Kālī* composed by the great master Bari is complete. [Endorsed by] the Nepalese Paṇḍita.
It was translated, edited, and finalized by the Indian master Ratnarakṣita and the Tibetan lotsāwa Rma Chos ’bar.
